speaker: Charly de Marez
talkTitle: Observing mesoscale dynamics at high latitudes in the SWOT era
abstract: For decades, classical altimetry has enabled global monitoring of mesoscale variability at midlatitudes, but only through gridded products that rely on spatiotemporal interpolation. This approach has now reached its limits when high resolution is required to investigate specific geophysical fluid dynamics (GFD) processes. The Surface Water and Ocean Topography (SWOT) mission marks the beginning of a new era, providing synoptic observations of ocean dynamics at scales below 100 km. In particular, at high latitudes, where the mesoscale is on the order of ~10-15 km and has been largely unobservable from space until now, SWOT provides the first satellite-based characterization of eddy regimes. We present the capabilities of SWOT for detecting high-latitude eddies and highlight its ability to capture both eddy-poor and eddy-rich regimes in polar and subpolar oceans. We also present case studies from the Labrador Sea and around Iceland, where SWOT-informed eddy detection has enabled targeted in situ sampling and high resolution numerical model validations. These results open the door to process-oriented numerical and experimental studies, offering new perspectives on the still poorly understood mesoscale dynamics at high latitudes.
bio: Charly de Marez completed a doctoral thesis at the Laboratoire d'Oceanographie Physique et Spatiale (LOPS) during which he specialized in the study of mesoscale vortices. He then extended his fields of interest during a post-doctoral contract at the California Institute of Technology in Pasadena, as part of NASA's SWOT satellite CalVal mission, where he studied surface ocean turbulence. He then moved to the University of Iceland in Reykjavik, to study the mesoscale circulation in the North Atlantic, and specifically around Iceland. He is now a CNRS researcher at LOPS, where he continues the study of mesoscale turbulence. His work combines satellite altimetry, in situ observations, and numerical modeling to study the dynamics, interactions, and impacts of these eddies, with a particular emphasis on high-latitude and polar regions.
